messages.subject_clean: Using a matrix as a sitecov to calculate occupancy
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I have been trying to use season (wet and dry) which is a Matrix (35 rows and 18 columns) as a site covariate to calculate occupancy. But it appears that unmarked does not accept a matrix as a site variable, so I tried putting my matrix covariate in the obscovs but I could only calculate detection. Does anyone know how can I use a matrix as a site cov??? The other site covs are each one a single column. Perhaps would be easier to use season as an observation covariate and then use it for occupancy. Any thoughts?

Here is the script I have been using:

library(unmarked)
dapu.covs <- read.csv("Covariates.csv")
dapu.covs2<-read.csv("Season.csv")

dapu.y <- DetHist$detection_history
sitecovs <- data.frame(veg=dapu.covs$veg,
                       distance=dapu.covs$distance)

factor.var<-data.frame(station=factor(dapu.covs$Station),pres_hum=factor(dapu.covs$pres_human), season=factor(dapu.covs2))

THEN I GET THIS ERROR:
Error in data.frame(station = factor(dapu.covs$station), pres_hum = factor(dapu.covs$pres_hum),  :
  arguments imply differing number of rows: 35, 18

Any help will be highly appreciated.

Thanks,
Angélica

messages.body_plain:
Hi Angélica,
First, a distinction must be made between the two types of covariates you can use in the static occupancy model: Site and survey (observation) covariates. Site covariates, as the name implies, are those that can vary between sites (spatial units). These covariates can affect both ecological (like habitat type) and observation process (camera model, observer experience).
In the case of survey covariates, they vary for each survey and in some cases for each site as well. These covariates only affect the detection process, for example, the moon phase, daily rain or temperature, among others.

Now, if you remember, the probability function of the occupancy model is psi is calculated for each site=  Zi ~ Bernoulli (psii) = where i is each sampling unit. Therefore, only site covariates are used to model it. Additionally, it must be remembered that the one season model assumes that the state of occupancy value for each site will not change during the sampling period (*can be relaxed). So, you cannot use a matrix as a site covariate to model psi.

Probably your best option is to migrate to a dynamic model, where you can evaluate the change in psi through various samplings or seasons. You can check the help of colext() function in unmarked.

I also recommend this paper, it helps me a lot to understand the basis of the models Guillera-Arroita 2017 Modeling of species distributions, range dynamics and communities under imperfect detection: advances, challenges and opportunities, which helped me a lot to understand how hierarchical models work.

Hope i have been helpful

messages.subject: Re: Is my dataset not compatible with unmarked?
messages.subject_clean: Is my dataset not compatible with unmarked?
messages.body_plain:
Sabina,

If you have 10 sites and 17 visits, then your site covariates would have 10 rows and your count data would have 17 columns and 10 rows.  Your observation data would have 17 * 10 rows.  The obs data corresponds to the repeat surveys and tends to include variables like observer, date, weather, etc.  Sounds like you're trying to use your data for the 200 sample locations as observation data?  If so, no, that shouldn't work.

One option for you is to use the 200 sample locations as your samples, so that your site covariates would have 200 rows.  You could then include 'site' as a covariate in your models, to account for differences among the 10 sites.  This would add 9 more coefficients to your model, which could be an issue given the amount of data you have, I'm not sure.  This would account for spatial correlation among the 20 samples at a site.  But if your objective is to learn specifics about different variables at your 10 sites, this method wouldn't tell you much.

This hierarchical arrangement of samples within sites is perfect for mixed models, but as I understand unmarked does not include mixed models yet.  But apparently it could be done with a Bayesian approach that I have no experience with.

Mike Worland

messages.subject_clean: Group and season-specific occupancy estimates using colext
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ken and others,

I have a follow up question. Is there a similar set of functions that could be used to calculate group-specific abundance estimates and CIs using the empirical Bayes posterior predictive distribution?

I am trying to do this using a capture recapture dataset with multinomPois models, but getting stuck at the prediction stage as the CIs coming out of the predict function (both SE*1.96 and the upper/lower) are very uniform, which doesn't seem right to me.

Thanks in advance

On Tuesday, March 31, 2020 at 7:41:34 AM UTC+11, Ken Kellner wrote:

> Hi,
>
> If I am understanding your question correctly, a potential alternative approach would be to use the empirical Bayes posterior predictive distribution. For some discussion see here:
>
> https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/qViR90-RHX4
>
> I wrote up a quick example based on the `colext` frog example below. In the future some of the functions I used will be built-in to unmarked (they already are in the dev version).
>
> library(unmarked)
>
> data(frogs)
> umf <- formatMult(masspcru)
> obsCovs(umf) <- scale(obsCovs(umf))
>
> ## Use 1/4 of data just for run speed in example
> umf <- umf[which((1:numSites(umf)) %% 4 == 0),]
>
> #Add fake site covariate as an example
> #takes values 'a' or 'b'
> siteCovs(umf) <- data.frame(fakeCov=factor(sample(c('a','b'), numSites(umf),
>                                     replace=T)))
> fm <- colext(psiformula = ~ fakeCov,
>              gammaformula = ~ fakeCov,
>              epsilonformula = ~ fakeCov,
>              pformula = ~ JulianDate + I(JulianDate^2), umf)
>
> # Empirical Bayes estimates of number of sites occupied in each year
> re <- ranef(fm)
>
> ########################################################################
> #These two functions below will be built-in in next version of unmarked
> #Sample from posterior
> postSamples <- function(object, nsims=100){
>
>   N <- dim(object@post)[1]
>   K <- dim(object@post)[2]
>   T <- dim(object@post)[3]
>
>   out <- array(NA, c(N, T, nsims))
>
>   for (n in 1:N){
>     for (t in 1:T){
>         out[n, t, ] <- sample(0:(K-1), nsims, replace=TRUE,
>                               prob=object@post[n,,t])
>     }
>   }
>   out
> }
>
> #predict method for ranef
> prRanef <- function(object, func, nsims=100){
>
>   ps <- postSamples(object, nsims=nsims)
>   s1 <- func(ps[,,1])
>   nm <- names(s1)
>   row_nm <- rownames(s1)
>   col_nm <- colnames(s1)
>
>   if(is.vector(s1)){
>     out_dim <- c(length(s1), nsims)
>   } else{
>     out_dim <- c(dim(s1), nsims)
>   }
>
>   param <- apply(ps, 3, func)
>
>   out <- array(param, out_dim)
>
>   if(is.vector(s1)){
>     rownames(out) <- nm
>   } else {
>     rownames(out) <- row_nm
>     colnames(out) <- col_nm
>   }

The same approach should work for abundance models also. Assuming you have the latest unmarked, see the following example with multinomPois:

library(unmarked)

data(ovendata)

set.seed(123)
sc <- as.data.frame(scale(ovendata.list$covariates[,-1]))
#Add dummy factor covariate
sc$facCov <- factor(sample(c("a","b"), nrow(sc), replace=TRUE))

#Create umf
ovenFrame <- unmarkedFrameMPois(ovendata.list$data,
  siteCovs=sc,
  type = "removal")

fm1 <- multinomPois(~ 1 ~ ufc + facCov, ovenFrame)

r <- ranef(fm1)

#Function to apply to each simulation
#Mean abundance by group
group_func <- function(x){
  out <- numeric(2)
  out[1] <- mean(x[sc$facCov=="a"])
  out[2] <- mean(x[sc$facCov=="b"])
  out
}

pr <- predict(r, func=group_func, nsims=100)
#output is 2 x nsims

#Get mean and 95% CIs
plot_inp <- data.frame(group=c("a","b"), mean=rowMeans(pr),
                       lower=apply(pr, 1, quantile, 0.025),
                       upper=apply(pr, 1, quantile, 0.975))

#Plot
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyverse)
plot_inp %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=group, y=mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=lower, ymax=upper), width=0.2) +
  geom_point(size=2) +
  labs(y="Mean abundance", x="Group")

Hi everyone,

I'd just like to emphasize that Ken's addition of a `predict` method for `ranef` objects is a great new feature that many users may not have noticed. It allows for posterior prediction using Empirical Bayes methods. In other words, you can compute predictive distributions for functions of latent variables such as abundance or occurrence. This is very useful for generating point estimates and confidence intervals for derived quantities such as total abundance in the surveyed region or the proportion of sites occupied.

Unlike the `predict` methods that have always been available, which focus on the *expected* values of abundance or occurrence, the Empirical Bayes `predict` methods focus on *realized* values of abundance and occurrence, which are specific to the sampled plots and conditional on the observed data. Both types of prediction are important for different objectives, but it wasn't until recently that the posterior prediction methods were added. Thanks Ken!

Richard

I was wondering if anyone else has dealt with spatial autocorrelation in track count surveys, and whether surveys need to be reasonably independent for accurate model fit. Any suggestions would be very much appreciated!

Rachael

Dear Rachel,

quite a standard sample design, but quite hard to properly analyse and interpret, I would say. Here are a couple of comments:

First of all, the Nmix model of Royle 2004 is probably not appropriate for your data, since it requires that each individual is only counted once. You count tracks, and I presume that it is quite possible that the same hare crosses the line multiple times within a 30m segment, thus violating this basic assumption, producing some sort of a false positive error. If you think that the problem of such multi-counting is quite common, then you *might* experiment with the Poisson-Poisson N-mixture model (see Stanley and Royle 2005, Guillera Arroita et al. 2011; also Section 6.13.2 in the AHM1 book), which does allow an individual to appear in a count multiple times. However, my own experience with this model is rather negative: it yielded what were deemed to be unrealistic estimates and I concluded that it is probably very sensitive to subtle violations of the parametric assumptions. Though of course in other situations it might perform OK.

If however you are quite confident that a hare can only be counted once per 30-m segment or perhaps if you actually follow their tracks and make sure that you only count once the hare with a track that crosses the line multiple times, then you should be fine in principle with the basic Nmix model.

If you can't exclude multiple counts and don't want to use the Poisson/Poisson Nmix model, then one of your usual fall-back positions would be some sort of Poisson GLMM, where you merely model intensity of use, which is the combination of abundance and detection rate that the Nmix models attempt to separate out. In GLMMs, it would be simple to account for non-independence of counts for 30-m segments within the same transect, either with or without spatial autocorrelation.

You could also account for spatial autocorrelation inside of an Nmix model; see Aing et al., JAPPL, 2011 (which is for an occupancy model, but for linear data along transects, and you could do the same thing also inside of an Nmix model). See Chapter 9 in our upcoming AHM2 book (very soon now !)

The other usual fall-back position for counts that are not "nmixable" are occupancy models, where you simply model presence or absence along a spatial unit. Especially if the abundance per unit is small, you may hardly lose anything by going from the modeling of abundance to that of presence/absence. About 10 years ago a couple of models were developed to account for spatial autocorrelation along trails, see these:

Guillera-Arroita, G., Morgan, B.J.T., Ridout, M.S. and Linkie, M. (2011). Species occupancy modelling for detection data collected along a transect. Journal of Agricultural, Biological and Environmental Statistics, 3, 301-317

Hello everyone,

My name is Rachael and I am a relatively new user of the unmarked package. I have been using the pcount function to estimate snowshoe hare abundance across habitat types over multiple winter seasons. My data are in the form of track counts; specifically, I have 1.5 km transects that were divided into 30m segments and I counted all tracks that crossed the transect line every 30m, within 48 hours of a snowfall. Snowshoe hare are nocturnal so these counts should reflect tracks from the previous 1-2 nights. These transects were conducted multiple (3-5) times per winter over four winter seasons. I plan to analyze each year separately to satisfy the assumption of a closed population.

I am unsure whether I am violating model assumptions, and if so, how severe these violations might be in terms of interpreting my model. I am currently coding every 30m segment as a "survey", and including the transect number (i.e. each 1.5 km transect) as a site covariate. However, there is likely some spatial autocorrelation between my surveys since hares almost certainly move >30m in a given night. I was wondering if anyone else has dealt with spatial autocorrelation in track count surveys, and whether surveys need to be reasonably independent for accurate model fit. Any suggestions would be very much appreciated!

Rachael
